doc.title: Rudy Van Gelder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Jimmy Smith dates, two-track versus multi-track, session problems
summary: He clarifies that Jimmy Smith's Blue Note work was two-track while Creed sessions were multi-track, which grew from eight to 48 tracks.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Well, we’ve covered a lot of it. Maybe you can say a little bit about what it was like when you’d have some of these larger sessions, back before the booze when you would have Oliver Nelson come in with a bunch of musicians and maybe he’s backing Jimmy Smith. About, you know, the challenges of…of—I guess it really wasn’t challenges; it’s just the way that what was called on for that day. To me it seems very challenging because there were a lot of musicians; you have to bring it into a two-track environment immediately.
Well we never had a large quantity of musicians on two-track. By that time I was in multi-track.
Multi-track, yeah. I know, I just mean the Jimmy Smith dates Oliver Nelson, those are direct to two-track. No.

No, the only two-track Jimmy Smith was at the remotes. I don’t remember tunes with two-tracks. The ones from Blue Note, whatever he did with Blue Note was two- track. Whenever he came over to Creed we had multi-track, we used multi-track. I don’t remember using two-track with Jimmy’s band. I wish I had sometime. When I used to go on vacation…
Okay we can scrap all of that then.
I’m just saying…Okay, cause I thought a lot of that was direct to two track.
What about that Bill Evans recording?

That’s not two-track. I mean, that may not have been 24 track, but it was multi- track somehow. I don’t know what I had at the time. That was during the period working with Creed, that I had the wherewithal and the motivation to develop multi-track for me. We started out with eight, and then we went to twelve, then 24, 48. 48 really tore it up, that really brought it all to a musical impasse. The fact that they had 48 tracks, what they could do with that. And now, of course, there’s no limit to the tracks. That’s a very anti- musical way to perform, I think. That’s my opinion. Yeah, I don’t like that, strike all that part its too negative, all right? Anything negative in there, just erase it.
Mhmm. Let’s see, what haven’t we talked about?

So every session there is some kind of problem, alright? Everything from tuning the piano, to somebody coming in with some problem, what’s wrong with that? That’s the way it is? You have to have the tools to be able to match what the problem is, and that’s what learning the studio is.
Yeah, I think that’s what I do.
